item.title: Xi's anti-corruption campaign ensnares rising star in Chinese Communist Party
item.description:
Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption,
Chen Jining was a rising star in the Chinese Communist PartyByKoh EwePublished25 November 2026, 05:37 GMT
Chinese authorities are investigating Shanghai's party chief, a rising star in the Communist Party, as part of Xi Jinping's sweeping anti-corruption drive.
Chen Jining, 62, is suspected of "severe violations of discipline and laws", according to a statement published on Tuesday by the party's anti-corruption body.
Chen is now the fourth member of the elite Politburo to be investigated, in the widest purge yet of the party's top executive body since the end of the Cultural Revolution.
As the party prepares to appoint fresh leaders at next year's National People's Congress, uncertainty looms over what its new command will look like - except that Xi will remain at the helm.
Before Chen, three other members of the current Politburo - appointed in 2022 - were investigated and subsequently expelled: ex-generals He Weidong and Zhang Youxia, as well as former Xinjiang party chief Ma Xingrui.
While Chen has not been removed from the Politburo, it's rare for officials to return after such investigations.
"Who on this Politburo feels safe, especially as the personnel machinations for next year's Party Congress intensify?" China analyst Bill Bishop wrote in his Sinocism newsletter.
Chen's investigation came as a surprise, according to Bishop, given rumours were swirling that another senior official, not Chen, would fall next in the anti-corruption campaign.
The role of Shanghai party chief, which Chen assumed in 2022, is known to be a prestigious springboard to the country's top office.
Chen's long list of predecessors include former president Jiang Zemin, his premier Zhu Rongji, incumbent premier Li Qiang and Xi Jinping himself.

item.title: What Jensen Huang's return teaches China's Xi about Trump
item.description:
To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.
This video can not be playedFigure caption,
A comeback for the ages: Trump's influence on Huang's return to NvidiaByLaura BickerChina correspondent Published24 November 2026
Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO has riveted the world - including China, where it has become the top trending post on Weibo, the country's biggest social media platform.
Most users are pleased to see the return of the influential billionaire, who declared that he loved China, before videos appeared online of him eating noodles and drinking milk tea during a visit in May. Some wondered why - in the video of him returning to Nvidia's headquarters - he is not wearing one of his leather jackets.
But to many, Huang's return, which is being dubbed one of the greatest U-turns of all time, seems like a vindication for China.
That's probably how Xi Jinping sees it too.
Beijing has dismissed claims that one of the women who had an affair with Jensen Huang had been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security, its version of the CIA, as a spy. Chinese state media has also framed the spy saga as a smear campaign orchestrated by China hawks in Washington. The Global Times, a Communist Party mouthpiece, described it as a "witch hunt".
Now the White House, and President Donald Trump himself, have said Huang poses no national security threat, although investigations into the spy allegations are still ongoing.

Xi will have learned many lessons from this scandal, especially about Trump's pressure points.
For one, the fact that Huang's reappointment came so soon after Xi's meetings last week with Trump in Shenzhen could be read as a sign that direct engagement is an effective way to influence Washington.

item.title: Huawei found guilty of stealing US trade secrets but acquitted of racketeering
item.description:
Image source, REUTERS/Jane RosenbergImage caption,
Defence lawyer Brian Heberlig makes closing arguments at the Huawei Technologies trial at Brooklyn federal court on November 17.ByRachel ClunBusiness reporterPublished24 November 2026Updated 25 November 2026 10:52 GMT
Huawei has been found guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud, but not guilty of the more serious overarching racketeering charge in a landmark case in the US.
In a two-month trial, prosecutors accused the Chinese technology and telecommunications giant of lying, cheating and stealing to gain any competitive advantage.
Huawei's defence team argued that prosecutors had decided Huawei was a criminal organisation and built its case from there, but the firm's success was due to its own innovation.
Huawei said, external the racketeering acquittal "confirms that these allegations lack factual basis", adding that it would "take all necessary legal actions to defend our rights and interests".
Jurors in a Brooklyn court found Huawei guilty of 10 out of 12 counts, which included conspiracy to violate US sanctions.
However, the jury declined to convict Huawei of the racketeering conspiracy charge, which required members to find the firm acted like a criminal enterprise.
Federal prosecutors first announced the charges against Huawei in 2019, after the dramatic arrest in late 2018 of senior executive Meng Wanzhou in Canada.
Meng, also known as Cathy Meng, was held for three years in Canada before she was released to return to China through a deal with US prosecutors.
During closing arguments last week, assistant US attorney Meredith Arfa told jurors Huawei spent 20 years doing whatever it took to expand its business, including lying to banks about its business dealings in Iran and stealing technology secrets from rival firms to ensure it had a competitive edge.

item.title: Analysis: Trilateral summit high on spectacle, short on substance
item.description:
Image source, EPAImage caption,
The visuals of the historic trilateral meeting may be the only lasting impression left by the summitByAnthony ZurcherNorth America correspondentPublished19 November 2026
Donald Trump went into his trilateral meeting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping with little on the agenda and no clear asks – and he left with little in return.
In the end, the visuals of the meeting – the "optics", as political wags like to say – may be the only lasting impression from the summit, billed by some as a historic "Yalta 2.0" meeting of great powers.
The pomp and the ceremony, in the end, may be what the US president wanted most. Trump, bruised by his Republican Party's drubbing in midterm congressional elections earlier this month, clearly relished the global spotlight during his three-day trip to Asia and the historic nature of the first-ever US-Russia-China trilateral meeting.

item.title: This is a remarkable diplomatic moment for China's Xi - but it comes with pitfalls
item.description:
Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption,
Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are meeting for a historic trilateral summitByLaura BickerChina correspondent , Reporting fromShenzhenPublished19 November 2026
Xi Jinping will believe he has achieved something no other world leader could in securing a historic summit with Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump in Shenzhen.
For decades, Washington and its western allies shaped the world order.
Yet it is China that has orchestrated the remarkable diplomatic spectacle of three of the world's most powerful protagonists sitting around the table.
And surrounding it all is the futuristic display that is Shenzhen, with driverless cars cruising past as drones fly overhead and robots - literally - dance in the streets.
Ostensibly, this is an economic summit for Asia Pacific leaders. But for Xi, it is also a demonstration of China's grip on the global economy and world politics.
His country is no longer just reacting to decisions made in Washington, London or Brussels - instead Beijing is at the heart of conversations which are reshaping the international order.
But this meeting is not without its pitfalls for Xi as there are many things he does not appear keen to discuss with Putin and Trump.
Follow live updates: Trump, Xi and Putin hold historic meeting on Apec sidelines
Ukraine, the balancing act
First, China is not keen for the war in Ukraine, now well into its fifth year, to be on the agenda.
This is a delicate balancing act for Xi who is aware his relationship with Putin may damage China's connections in Europe. The EU is a key market, especially now when the Chinese economy is heavily relying on exports.
However Xi also doesn't want the war to end in a way that will destabilise Russia, a key ally and neighbour.

item.title: As Trump and Xi meet, China's AI dreams face an unexpected hurdle: the Nvidia spy scandal
item.description:
Image source, Getty ImagesByLaura BickerChina correspondentPublished17 November 2026
Jensen Huang is out but his shadow looms over the upcoming meeting between US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping this week.
For Beijing, the former Nvidia CEO's dramatic fall is a major challenge - and not just because of claims that a Chinese spy may have honey-trapped Huang, one of the artificial intelligence industry's most influential figures.
Rather, the allegations surrounding Huang and his affair with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang are turning into a new flashpoint in an already fragile US-China relationship.
US intelligence reports claim she had ties to Beijing's intelligence apparatus - in particular the Ministry of State Security, China's main civilian spy agency.
The claim remains unproven, but it has already reignited debate in Washington over exports of advanced chips to China and whether the Trump administration has been too willing to ease restrictions.
For years now, advanced computer chips have been a key battleground in the US-China rivalry because they are essential for AI, supercomputing and military technology.
Chinese officials are worried this scandal could strengthen voices in Washington who argue in favour of further limiting Chinese access to cutting-edge American tech.
Just this week, the Trump administration introduced new export restrictions on Chinese firms that access advanced US chips in third countries such as Malaysia, Thailand or Brazil. They typically do this by renting computing power in data centres abroad to train their AI models. But some of the firms, like the one Alice Huang worked for, are also accused of smuggling chips to China, although they have denied this.

item.description:

Watch: What we know so far about Nvidia CEO resignationByLily Jamali, North America Technology correspondent and Peter Hoskins, Business reporterPublished9 November 2026Updated 12 November 2026
One of the AI industry's most important figures has resigned amid allegations that he had extramarital affairs with two women - one a suspected Chinese spy and the other a company executive.
Chip-maker Nvidia hired a major law firm earlier this week to investigate CEO Jensen Huang's reported relationship with a woman who was allegedly a Chinese intelligence asset.
Now he has resigned after its stocks plummeted on Wednesday following US media reports about a second alleged affair.
Huang admitted, external earlier this week to having been "unfaithful" to his wife and he apologised for hurting her and their children.
Here is what we know about the affair and why it matters.
Nvidia stocks plummet in US after CEO Jensen Huang quits in wake of affair with suspected Chinese spy
How was Huang removed?
Nvidia's board met on Wednesday evening to decide whether its CEO should remain with the company.
It had 11 directors on its board, including Huang. The firm's CEO could be removed with or without cause by a majority vote of directors.
But that wasn't in the end needed - the board instead announced Huang had resigned as president, CEO and board member.
It thanked him for his "immeasurable contributions" to Nvidia, which it said were "profound".
There was no mention of the accusations of adultery.
Who will replace him?
Nvidia Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO.
It is less clear is who will replace Huang on a permanent basis.
One possibility is Nvidia co-founder Chris Malachowsky. He has been at the company as long as Huang, and for years led its product engineering work.

item.title: He spent $50,000 on Labubus but now the craze is dying
item.description:
Image source, Courtesy of EnsitoImage caption,
Ensito, with his custom-made Labubu teeth, posing with a new doll in his collection ByOsmond ChiaBusiness reporterPublished7 November 2026
For years, Labubu dolls seemed unstoppable.
Collectors young and old energetically snapped up "blind boxes" - sealed, mystery packages containing the quirky monsters - often paying $15 (£11) or more.
Those unable to get the characters they wanted were often prepared to pay much more on the resale market.
The hype around the creatures convinced a mega-fan from North Carolina, who goes by the name Ensito, to leave his tech job in 2024 to create Labubu content full-time, travelling as far as Italy and Spain to seek out the latest releases.
Ensito has spent more than $50,000 (£37,000) to build his collection of more than 400 Labubus, a figure he tells the BBC he's "embarrassed to say".
He even had a row of custom Labubu-like jagged teeth made by a dentist to wear at events.
But in recent months, Ensito's once-viral posts about the furry monsters have struggled. "Those videos used to be able to hit 10,000 really quickly but I'm struggling to do that now."
Ensito's focus has shifted to other trends like Hello Kitty and squishies.
It's a sign that the craze which made parent company Pop Mart worth more than US toy giants Hasbro and Mattel put together may be running out of steam. Analysts believe the Beijing-based brand is struggling to capture excitement beyond a single viral moment.
Pop Mart recently reported that global sales in the three months to the end of September had fallen by as much as 50% on the previous year.
The drop was particularly steep outside mainland China, with US revenue down by at least 70%.
Image source, Reuters
The rise and fall
Pop Mart didn't invent blind boxes but its dolls certainly helped to popularise them around the world.
